questions.prompt: In the 3-bit marble counter, how many distinct values can the register hold before it must wrap around?
questions.explanation: 3 bits give 2^3 = 8 distinct patterns: 000 through 111, i.e. 0 through 7.

questions.prompt: What happens physically when the 3-bit marble counter is at 111 (7) and one more marble drops?
options: All three gear-bits flip back to 000 at once
Only the rightmost bit flips, giving 110
questions.answer: All three gear-bits flip back to 000 at once
questions.explanation: This is a carry ripple: 111 + 1 = 1000 in binary, but only 3 bits exist, so the overflow bit is lost and all three flip to 0.

questions.prompt: In the Token Grid State Machine, what does the pointer do on every single step?
options: Compares the whole row against itself
Randomly picks two cells to compare
questions.explanation: Bubble sort's pointer only ever looks at one adjacent pair (index i and i+1) per step.

questions.prompt: After ONE full left-to-right pass of the Token Grid State Machine, where does the largest value in the row always end up?
questions.explanation: Because the pointer always swaps a bigger left neighbor past a smaller right neighbor, the largest value keeps getting swapped rightward until it reaches the end of the pass.

questions.prompt: In the Mechanical Stream Comparator, what triggers the interceptor?
options: Two consecutive marbles having different values
Any marble with an even value
The stream running out of marbles
Two consecutive marbles having the same value
questions.answer: Two consecutive marbles having different values
questions.explanation: The comparator watches neighboring pairs and trips the interceptor the first time a pair disagrees.

questions.prompt: Once the interceptor in the Stream Comparator has tripped, what happens to later marbles in the same run?
options: Nothing — the circuit stays tripped, later marbles are never checked
It resets automatically and keeps checking
It only ignores marbles equal to the last one
questions.answer: Nothing — the circuit stays tripped, later marbles are never checked
questions.explanation: A physical interceptor, once triggered, blocks the ramp — it doesn't reset mid-run. The comparator halts at the first mismatch.

questions.prompt: Why does this module use physical/tactile machines (Turing Tumble, token grids) before writing any code?
options: So the underlying mechanism is felt and seen before it's abstracted into symbols
Because code is more error-prone than gears
Because Python can't express binary counting
It's purely decorative and has no teaching purpose
questions.answer: So the underlying mechanism is felt and seen before it's abstracted into symbols
questions.explanation: Concrete-before-abstract is the core idea of this on-ramp: you build the intuition with something you can touch, then re-express the exact same logic in code.

questions.prompt: In binary, what does each additional bit do to the number of representable values?
questions.explanation: Each bit is a independent 0/1 choice, so n bits give 2^n combinations — one more bit always doubles the count.

questions.prompt: What is the largest value a 3-bit register can hold?
questions.explanation: With 3 bits, values run 0 to 2^3 - 1 = 7. 8 would need a 4th bit.

questions.prompt: In the Token Grid State Machine's bubble sort, is a comparison the same thing as a swap?
options: No — a comparison happens every step, a swap only happens if the left value is bigger
Yes, every comparison is also a swap
No — swaps happen every step, comparisons are optional
They only differ when the row has duplicates
questions.answer: No — a comparison happens every step, a swap only happens if the left value is bigger
questions.explanation: Every step is a comparison; only some comparisons (when out of order) trigger a swap. An already-sorted row has comparisons but zero swaps.
